items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the public health law, in relation to prevention and screening
for elevated lead levels in children
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S5024

SPONSOR: RIVERA
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public health law, in relation to prevention and
screening for elevated lead levels in children

 
PURPOSE:

To establish a comprehensive system of preventive measures that prevent
and address instances of elevated blood lead levels in children.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 proclaims this act to be known as Dakota's Law.

Section 2 amends public health law and requires the following to be
included as part of the lead poisoning prevention program: - That prima-
ry health care providers shall provide the parent or guardian of each
child under six years of age anticipatory guidance on lead poisoning
prevention as part of routine care, including but not limited to their
right to an inspection if the child is at risk of lead exposure.

Section 3 amends public health law to require every primary health care
provider to conduct a lead exposure risk assessment questionnaire at
each routine well-child visit, or at least annually if a child has not
had routine well-child visits from when the child is at least six months
through the age of six.

Section 4 amends public health law to include pre-kindergarten and
kindergarten institutions as it relates to lead screening requirements
and the requirement to provide a parent or guardian with information on
lead poisoning if adequate lead screening has not been performed.

Section 5 amends public health law to grant pre-kindergarten insti-
tutions access to statewide immunization information system and the
blood lead information in such system and the citywide immunization
registry for the purpose of confirming an enrolling student has been
screened for lead and for the provision of appropriate educational mate-
rials when said student has elevated blood lead levels.

Section 6 provides for the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

This is bill 1 of 3 of Dakota's Law. Dakota's Law strengthens current
legislation to address signs of lead poisoning in all children proac-
tively. Currently in New York State, a child is considered to have
elevated blood lead levels if they are found to have 5 micrograms or
more per deciliter of whole blood but are only expected to be tested at
12 and 24 months. According to the World Health Organization, a child
reaching 10 micrograms faces developmental toxicity, or permanent
damage, due to lead exposure. The United States Center for Disease
Control recently changed their "blood lead levels of concern" from 10 to
5 micrograms, so that taking action at 5 micrograms can help families
address the cause of exposure before the permanent effects of this
preventable health condition are realized. Now that New York State has

confirmed their laws to CDC recommendations, we will ensure we create a
system where the state is proactive in exacting preventative measures.

This bill is part of a 3-bill package that includes the above prevention
centered legislation, legislation as it relates to insurance coverage,
and legislation to reflect the governor's language regarding "lead safe"
residential rental properties.  Dakota's Law originated from the mother
of Dakota, a child living in a NYCHA apartment who experienced increas-
ing blood lead levels throughout her childhood. Dakota's mother took
Dakota to the doctor and received appropriate testing at the required
ages, 12- and 24- months old. Upon changing doctors at age 4, she was
offered a lead screening and within this time frame, Dakota's blood lead
levels elevated from 5 micrograms to 45. This left Dakota with permanent
developmental challenges that affect her education. If this bill had
been law at the time, Dakota would have received a required test at age
3 and steps would have been taken earlier to identify and address the
lead exposure in her home before it became detrimental to her health.

This 3-bill package prompts healthcare professionals, state and local
health officers, and housing officials to take a proactive approach to
prevent permanent damage to a child's health and development from lead
exposure. In particular, this bill requires healthcare providers to
annually screen each child under 6 years old, triggering any action set
forth to provide a parent or guardian with adequate guidance on lead
poisoning prevention. Young children are more vulnerable to lead expo-
sure and more likely to develop permanent damage if exposed, including
developmental delay, learning difficulties, hearing loss, seizures, loss
of appetite, and irritability. Children are exposed through breathing in
or ingesting lead paint or other materials, including lead dust in their
environment, and younger children face increased risks of elevated blood
lead levels since their bodies are still developing, specifically their
neurological and digestive systems, making them more susceptible to
absorption of this toxic material. Since lead can be hard to detect in
their environment, children need to be screened and tested throughout
the critical first years of brain and body development and ensure that
the first signs of lead exposure are addressed, rather than waiting
until their blood lead levels are damaging.

Older children whose exposure or poisoning may have gone undetected also
deserve access to testing to address any exposure they encountered and
to assess any educational needs developed as a result of being left
undiagnosed. This 3-bill package addresses all of the preventative meas-
ures providing that lead screening and testing be available for all
children in New York State by expanding parameters for private health
insurance coverage and Medicaid coverage to include these preventive
services and to prohibit any copays and annual deductibles on these
services. All children and their families should have access to these
services so that we can eradicate sources of lead exposure and poisoning
and fully grasp its extent.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2019-2020: S499B/A7687 Peoples-Stokes.

2018: S9131/No Same-As.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.
